sections.h2: Who handles property tax at the courthouse
sections.html:
Todd County puts its tax work in one building: the courthouse at 202 East Washington Street in Elkton. All three offices answer through the county switchboard at (270) 265-9966, each on its own extension.

  • Sheriff, ext. 208: takes payment of property tax bills. The sheriff's website lets owners view their bills online but not pay them, so ask the office which payment methods it accepts.
  • Property Valuation Administration (PVA), ext. 504: the place to ask about the value of a property and to dispute it.
  • County clerk, ext. 501: registers vehicles and, after April 15, runs the delinquent-tax process.

The City of Elkton keeps a separate property tax payment link on its own website. If your address is inside the city, ask whether a city bill exists in addition to the county bill.

Todd County spans 377 square miles, and almost none of it is water. The cities are Elkton, Guthrie and Trenton, with Allensville and Fairview (mostly in Christian County) as census-designated places. Muhlenberg, Logan and Christian counties border Todd, as do Robertson and Montgomery counties in Tennessee. The county runs on Central time and has a single public school district, the Todd County School District.

Farming is a long-standing tradition. The southern lowlands, with Pembroke soil, are known for strong crop yields, and the northern high country is steeper, with oak, walnut and poplar. Buyers of rural property often care about the land as much as the house.

The county has 12,972 residents as of July 2025, a 5.9 percent rise since 2020, after a small slide during the 2010s. Population has hovered near 12,000 for decades. The housing figures matter most to a seller.

In 2020, 10.8 percent of housing units were vacant and 30.0 percent of occupied homes were rented. The trip to work averages 27.8 minutes. Vacant and rented houses are a visible part of the market, so an owner of an empty or tenant-occupied house has plenty of company.

The sheriff's file closes at the end of the day on April 15. Whatever is unpaid moves to the clerk's office, where a recorded lien attaches and the bill is renamed a certificate of delinquency. Until then the state schedule sets the price: 2 percent off if you pay by November 1, the bare amount through year end, a 5 percent surcharge in January and 10 percent afterward, with the sheriff's add-on fee on top.

Once the bill reaches the clerk, monthly interest of one percent runs, and commissions for the clerk and the county attorney follow. Waiting adds money fast, and the attorney's commission is waived only during the first five-business-day window after the transfer.

Under KRS 134.128 the sale falls 90 to 135 days after the sheriff hands bills to the clerk, a window the Department of Revenue puts at July 14 to August 28 on a regular schedule. Each year the clerk lists the sequence in order: a half-page notice, the published list, the deadline for outside buyers to register, and the sale itself, which begins at 9 AM.

A buyer of up to three bills registers with the county, while anyone wanting more than three registers with the state. A buyer of a bill gets a lien, not the house. Afterward the owner settles with that buyer, who may pile on costs. The county attorney mails notices to owners beforehand, and the list runs in the newspaper roughly a month before the sale.

sections.h2: If your bill has already been sold
sections.html:
An outside buyer who bought your bill holds a lien on the property, not the house itself. That lien still has to be paid before a sale can close, so the buyer's payoff becomes part of your closing figures. Ask the clerk at extension 501 who bought it and how to reach them, then request a written payoff that shows interest and any added costs.

If the sale has not happened yet, you can usually still pay at the clerk's office and stop the process. The county attorney's notices come first, and the published list gives you roughly a month of warning. Use that month. A bill paid at the clerk costs less than the same bill after an investor adds charges.

Valuation questions go to the PVA in the courthouse, extension 504. A conference there is mandatory. File the appeal at the clerk's office on the workday after the May viewing period ends. A panel of area owners then holds hearings a few weeks later.

The panel wants evidence: nearby sales, an appraisal, construction costs or insurance records. An owner who skips the local step or the hearing cannot continue to the Kentucky Claims Commission. Paid representatives must be professionals such as attorneys, accountants, brokers or appraisers and must hold written authorization.

For 2025 and 2026 the state lets an owner past 65, or totally disabled, subtract $49,100 from the assessed value of a home they live in. The Todd County PVA takes applications through December 31. The benefit stays with the owner, so a buyer files again.

Before closing, get the sheriff's payoff and ask the clerk about older certificates. Delinquent tax is the personal debt of the January 1 owner, and its lien can last eleven years, so a title agent will want a clean record before releasing funds.

Start at the courthouse. Ask the sheriff at extension 208 for the current figure, the clerk at extension 501 whether any year has gone to a certificate, and the PVA at extension 504 whether your exemption is on file. If your house is inside Elkton, add a call to the city about its bill. Put the figures together before you accept an offer, so you know the net you would walk away with. A cash buyer can take the house as is, and the tax balances come out of the proceeds at closing.

Bring a photo ID, the parcel number and the property address to the courthouse. If you hold the property through an estate, bring the paperwork showing who may sign for it. The closing agent will want to see that the person selling has authority to do so.

Allow a few days for each office to respond.

faqs.q: Where is a Todd County property tax bill paid?
faqs.a: At the sheriff's office inside the courthouse at 202 East Washington Street, extension 208 of (270) 265-9966. The sheriff's website lets you view bills, and the office can tell you which payment methods it takes.

faqs.q: Who reviews a Todd County assessment I disagree with?
faqs.a: The PVA, at extension 504. Ask for a conference first, because the local board hears only owners who have had one.

faqs.q: What is the Todd County homestead deduction?
faqs.a: The amount is $49,100 through the 2026 tax period, available to owners past 65 or totally disabled. Applications go to the PVA before the year ends.

faqs.q: Can an investor buy my delinquent Todd County bill?
faqs.a: Yes. After April 15 the bill sits at the clerk's office, and an outside purchaser can buy it at the yearly sale and then collect from you.

faqs.q: Can a Todd County house with unpaid tax be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance comes out of the sale price. Get written payoffs from the sheriff and clerk so the buyer's closing agent sees no surprises.
